entry.title: [ag-psd] ag-psd can exhaust memory when parsing crafted PSD dimensions
entry.content:
Summary

readPsd() commits the image/layer buffers from the declared header geometry (width x height x channels x depth, and per-layer rectangles) before validating those values against the actual data. A tiny crafted PSD declaring huge geometry forces a multi-gigabyte allocation.

Impact

On ag-psd 30.2.0, Node 24, a 52-byte PSD makes readPsd(buf) commit ~3.17 GB (measured peak RSS) in ~0.45 s before throwing a catchable RangeError ("Offset is outside the bounds of the DataView") — about 61,000,000x amplification. Because the buffer is committed before validation, the allocation OOM-kills the process before the error on essentially any host (uncatchable), and concurrent requests exhaust memory. Any service reading untrusted PSDs with ag-psd is exposed to a remote DoS.

This is distinct from #39 and #206, which involve genuinely large PSDs (memory proportional to real data). Here the input is 52 bytes: the file declares enormous geometry that is never present, so the allocation is driven by an unvalidated header field, not by actual content, an uncontrolled-allocation denial-of-service vulnerability, not proportional memory use.

Steps to reproduce

The PoC is a 52-byte PSD (sha256 a1146a6fabdfef289472f99a56851249e7a46e8d19d4d8bf85fe833e2f0158b6). Reconstruct with:

base64 -d > poc.psd <<'EOF'
OEJQUwABAAAAAAAAAA0AADcuAAA58wAgAAMAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAdEgNZv+i9bc9ygd2A==
EOF

Then (commits ~3.17 GB before throwing a catchable RangeError):

const { readPsd } = require('ag-psd');
const buf = require('fs').readFileSync('poc.psd');
readPsd(buf.buffer.slice(buf.byteOffset, buf.byteOffset + buf.byteLength));

Root cause

psdReader.js sizes the off-heap typed-array buffers from the declared header dimensions (and per-layer rectangles, a second independent lever) before validating against the available bytes.

Suggested fix

Validate the declared dimensions, channel count, depth, and per-layer rectangles against the actual input length (and a sane maximum) before allocating.

References

  • https://github.com/Agamnentzar/ag-psd/security/advisories/GHSA-qfx6-q44v-9qqw

  • https://github.com/Agamnentzar/ag-psd/tree/31.0.0

entry.title: [@sveltejs/adapter-static] SvelteKit: Prerendered paths are interpreted as regular expressions in Vercel route config generated by @sveltejs/adapter-vercel and @sveltejs/adapter-static

entry.title: [@nuxt/nitro-server] Nuxt: Incomplete fix for GHSA-9v7c-q64q-vv33: a leading `//` in the request path bypasses `server/middleware` path checks and server route rules on page routes
entry.content:
Summary

Since 4.6.0, Nuxt parses a request path that starts with // as a URL with a host before rendering a page, so //x/admin renders the page at /admin. Nitro's routing, Nitro's route rules and server/middleware see the path as //x/admin, so server-side checks keyed on /admin do not apply. The fix for GHSA-9v7c-q64q-vv33 in 4.6.3 covered dot segments but not this form.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass server-side controls that match on the request path of a page route.

A route-scoped server handler is skipped:

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  serverHandlers: [{ route: '/admin', middleware: true, handler: '~~/server/admin-guard.ts' }],
})

// server/admin-guard.ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (!isAuthenticated(event)) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 401 })
  }
})

With this handler, /admin returns 401, but //x/admin and ///x/admin render app/pages/admin.vue along with the data it fetches during server rendering. server/middleware that checks event.path.startsWith('/admin') is skipped in the same way.

Server-side redirect and headers route rules are also skipped, so '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' } does not redirect //x/admin/secret, and per-route security headers such as Content-Security-Policy are not sent.

Browsers send a path such as //x/admin as written, so a plain link is enough to reach the page.

Not affected:

  • API handlers in server/api and server/routes, which Nitro does not match for these paths.
  • appMiddleware route rules and middleware declared with definePageMeta, which are matched against the resolved route.
  • Nuxt 3.x and 4.0.0 to 4.5.x, which pass the path to the page router unchanged, so these requests 404.

Patches

Fixed in @nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4, which nuxt@4.6.4 depends on. The renderer now uses the request path exactly as Nitro matched it, so a path starting with // no longer resolves to a different page.

Workarounds

Reject request paths that start with // in a server middleware:

// server/middleware/double-slash.ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (event.path.startsWith('//')) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404 })
  }
})

A reverse proxy or CDN that merges repeated slashes before forwarding the request also removes the mismatch.

Credits

Nuxt thanks @kq5y for reporting this issue.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-r99w-jh2x-3mg9
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128077
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/75c12c6fb4c22ec2cbde0051da24776d2dffa868
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/releases/tag/v4.6.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r99w-jh2x-3mg9

entry.title: [@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http] OpenTelemetry JavaScript: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http
entry.content:
Summary

@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http redacts sensitive URL query parameters on outgoing (client) spans but not on incoming (server) spans. The server-span path writes the raw query string verbatim into the url.query attribute, so credentials embedded in inbound request URLs — AWS presigned-URL signatures, Azure SAS tokens (sig), GCS signed-URL signatures — are exported in plaintext to the configured tracing backend.

Configuring the redactedQueryParams option does not change this, as this applies only to outgoing (client) spans.

Impact

Information disclosure / credential leakage (CWE-200; CWE-532, insertion of sensitive information into telemetry data).

Who is impacted: any Node.js service instrumented with @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http — directly or transitively via @opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node — that receives inbound requests carrying credentials in the query string. Common cases: services fronting presigned S3/GCS downloads, Azure SAS-token URLs, and signature-authenticated webhooks.

Consequence: clients' still-valid credentials are written into server spans and stored by the tracing backend, readable by anyone with span-read access — observability vendor infrastructure, dashboard users, and internal audiences far broader than the credential's intended scope. Presigned-URL signatures typically remain valid for minutes to days after capture, so this is not merely historical exposure.

Severity: Moderate. Exploitation requires read access to the telemetry backend, and inbound URLs must actually carry signed credentials. However, the gap is a documented mitigation that silently fails to apply, which defeats the mitigation operators would reach for.

Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http version 0.222.0. Known sensitive query string values (as defined by Semantic Conventions) are redacted by default from span data for incoming spans. The redactedQueryParamsServer configuration option was added for customization.

References

  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js/security/advisories/GHSA-3v2p-hm54-8qcq
  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js/commit/e086dec7f9304107ef6d50b5877be88895c06aa7

entry.title: [astro] Astro: XSS via attribute injection in dynamic tag names
entry.content:
Summary

When a dynamic tag (const Tag = ...; <Tag />) resolves to a string, Astro renders it as a raw HTML element name. The name was filtered to remove characters that could inject attributes, but the filter did not handle /. Because HTML parsers treat / inside a tag as an attribute separator, a tag name such as img/src/onerror=alert(1) was rendered as an <img> element with an onerror attribute. The JSX renderer used for MDX did not filter string tag names at all.

For example:

---
const Tag = Astro.url.searchParams.get('as') ?? 'div';
---
<Tag>hello</Tag>

rendered ?as=img/src/onerror=alert(1) as live HTML.

Impact

Reflected or stored cross-site scripting, but only in applications that use untrusted input (such as a request parameter or an uncontrolled CMS field) as all or part of an element name. Astro itself never derives element names from request data.

Applications that let content choose an element should map that input to a fixed set of known tags. Letting untrusted input choose an element name is unsafe even with a correct filter, because it can still select elements such as script or iframe.

Affected versions

astro <= 7.4.4.

Patches

Fixed in astro 7.4.5. String tag names in .astro dynamic tags, JSX, and MDX now render only the leading valid element name, so characters such as / or = can no longer change the generated markup. Strings that do not start with a valid element name now throw an error.

Workarounds

Upgrade to astro 7.4.5 or later. Before upgrading, do not use untrusted input as an element name, or map it to a fixed set of known tags.

Credits

Reported by @uttej-badwane.

References

  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-mh32-jxcr-mh9f
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126361
  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/pull/18520
  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/commit/e023abac912d7cb6af2b9fb5107ef5dabc667096
  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/releases/tag/astro@7.4.5
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mh32-jxcr-mh9f

entry.title: [astro] Astro: Image endpoint in @astrojs/node can read files from a case-variant sibling of the output directory on case-sensitive filesystems
entry.content:
Summary

The /_image endpoint used by the @astrojs/node adapter checks that a requested local image is inside the build output directory before reading it from disk. That check compared paths case-insensitively. On case-sensitive filesystems (such as Linux), a directory whose path differs from the output directory only by letter case is a different directory, but it passed the check.

For example, with the client output directory at /srv/app/dist/client/, a request such as:

/_image?href=/../../DIST/client/secret.png&w=32&f=png

resolved to /srv/app/DIST/client/secret.png and was served, even though that file is outside the output directory.

Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read image files from outside the output directory, but only when all of the following are true:

  • The site uses on-demand rendering with the @astrojs/node adapter.
  • The server runs on a case-sensitive filesystem.
  • A directory exists whose path matches the output directory except for letter case (for example DIST/client next to dist/client). Such a layout is unusual, and the attacker cannot create it.

Only files the image service accepts can be read. Raster images are returned after resizing; SVG files are returned unchanged. Other file types fail during processing. Plain path traversal outside the output directory (for example /../../secret.png) was already rejected and is not affected.

Affected versions

astro >= 5.14.3, <= 7.4.6, when used with @astrojs/node (all versions up to 11.1.11). The vulnerable image endpoint is provided by astro and used by the @astrojs/node adapter.

Patches

Fixed in astro 7.4.7. The path check now compares paths exactly, and only ignores letter case for Windows drive-letter paths. The fix ships in astro, so upgrading @astrojs/node alone is not enough.

Workarounds

Upgrade to astro 7.4.7 or later. Before upgrading, make sure no directory next to the build output directory has a path that differs from it only by letter case.

Credits

Reported by @zachariah-mithani.

References

  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-r3h5-4585-7x3w
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126364
  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/commit/7da442bb286e0c29e1c9e1add6727b7cbf434f1a

entry.title: [@nuxt/schema] Nuxt dev server serves files from a parent directory with a stray lockfile or workspace file
entry.content:
Summary

Nuxt can pick a parent directory that does not declare a workspace as its default workspaceDir: the farthest directory with a lockfile when the project is not inside a git repository, or the farthest directory with a pnpm-workspace.yaml or deno.json file, even one that only holds settings. The Vite dev server allows /_nuxt/@fs/ requests for any file under workspaceDir. A stray lockfile or settings file in a parent directory, such as the home directory, therefore lets anyone who can reach the dev server read files in that directory and everything below it.

Impact

This affects the development server only; production builds are not affected. All of the following have to hold:

  • A parent directory contains either:
    • a lockfile (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, bun.lock and similar), while the project is not inside a git repository and has no workspace file (pnpm-workspace.yaml, turbo.json, lerna.json and similar) above it. Running npm install once in the home directory is enough to create one there.
    • a pnpm-workspace.yaml without a packages list (for example one that only holds pnpm settings such as onlyBuiltDependencies), or a deno.json or deno.jsonc without a workspace field. This applies even if the project is inside a git repository.
  • The dev server is reachable from the network (nuxt dev --host, nuxt dev --tunnel, a published container port, or a proxy onto the dev port). The default localhost bind limits this to local processes, which can usually read the same files directly.

For example, with ~/package-lock.json and a project at ~/projects/app that has no .git directory, nuxt dev --host serves GET /_nuxt/@fs/<home>/.ssh/id_ed25519 with status 200. Any file in the home directory that is not covered by Vite's server.fs.deny list can be read this way, including SSH keys, cloud credentials and the Nuxt DevTools auth token in ~/.nuxt/devtools/dev-auth-token.txt.

No browser is involved: a plain HTTP client is enough. A web page on another origin cannot read the response, and DNS rebinding is rejected by Vite's host check.

Projects whose parent directories contain none of these files are not affected, nor are projects inside a git repository whose only lockfile is their own. Nuxt 3.5.0 and later are affected.

Patches

Fixed in @nuxt/schema 4.6.4, which nuxt 4.6.4 depends on. A parent directory now only becomes the default workspaceDir if it declares a workspace: a pnpm-workspace.yaml with packages, a deno.json or deno.jsonc with workspace, a lerna.json, turbo.json or rush.json, a package.json with workspaces, or a git repository. A lockfile or a settings file alone no longer widens the dev server's server.fs.allow list. If your monorepo root is not detected this way, set workspaceDir in nuxt.config.ts. Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

Workarounds

Set workspaceDir explicitly in nuxt.config.ts to the project root (or to the real monorepo root), or remove the stray lockfile or settings file from the parent directory. Do not expose the dev server to untrusted networks. If the dev port was reachable from an untrusted network while this layout was in place, treat files in the parent directory as exposed and rotate credentials such as SSH keys and cloud tokens.

Credits

Nuxt thanks @superboy-zjc for the report.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-mjrq-cffv-q4qc
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/89d3306d1976dd52ac2e73078806a3e889cbb8bd
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/releases/tag/v4.6.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mjrq-cffv-q4qc

entry.title: [hono] Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
entry.content:
Summary

csrf() validates a request only when its Content-Type is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (<a ping>) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type text/ping, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and Content-Type: text/ping.

A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The csrf() options for origin and secFetchSite do not change the outcome, because neither header is evaluated for the request.

The request body is fixed, so only actions whose effect does not depend on the body can be triggered. Firefox does not send pings by default. As with any CSRF, the user's cookie must be sent with the request, which with the default SameSite=Lax means a same-site origin or a cookie set with SameSite=None.

Impact

A user who visits a malicious page in Chrome or Edge while logged in to an application protected by csrf() can be made to send a state-changing request to that application, such as logging out, deleting a resource, or toggling a setting that is selected by the path or query string.

This issue affects applications that rely on csrf() as their CSRF protection and expose state-changing endpoints whose effect does not depend on the request body.

Workarounds

Reject requests with a Content-Type of text/ping in a middleware registered before csrf(), or set session cookies with SameSite=Strict.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-46wx-v44x-9hh2
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/bf16471913b5199212dac33f5d170f94745dd26a
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-46wx-v44x-9hh2

entry.title: [hono] Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
entry.content:
Summary

validator('form') only recognizes a multipart/form-data Content-Type that carries nothing but a single boundary parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as charset, or with extra whitespace after the ; is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while c.req.parseBody() still parses the body as a form.

Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole Content-Type value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like ; boundary=... fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through c.req.parseBody() or c.req.formData().

application/x-www-form-urlencoded is not affected. Only the multipart/form-data branch has the strict pattern.

This issue arises when an application relies on validator('form') to reject or restrict fields and the validation callback does not fail on an empty object.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can send form fields that the form validator never sees, by adding a legal parameter to the Content-Type header.

This may lead to:

  • Allow-list or required-field checks in the validator being skipped
  • Fields the application intended to reject reaching the handler

This issue affects applications that use validator('form') with multipart/form-data requests and whose validation callback accepts an empty object.

Workarounds

Reject an empty object in the validator('form') callback, or validate the result of await c.req.parseBody() in the handler.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-4h7h-rv7c-7m2v
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/d88fab372415277a9e540e895650943dd08eef4a
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4h7h-rv7c-7m2v

entry.title: [hono] Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
entry.content:
Summary

mount() and app.mount() remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on /app/admin/*. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

Details

  1. Dynamic prefix (all affected versions): for a mount such as /api/:tenant/*, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so /api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret reaches the mounted application as /admin/secret.
  2. Re-normalization (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to url.pathname, which turns a decoded backslash into / and collapses ... /app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret reaches the mounted application as /admin/secret.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as /assets*. A trailing slash in an app.mount() prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use mount() or app.mount() and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

References
